name: parameter_awareness
description: Guidance on understanding, choosing, and documenting bioinformatics parameters.
---

# Parameter Awareness

Start from a defensible baseline, change parameters only for a stated
reason, and treat every change as a testable analytical choice.

## Expected Workflow

- **1. Establish the dataset facts first**:
  - data layout
  - assay type
  - reference genome
  - control availability
  - library-preparation metadata
  - obvious signals of sparse, noisy, or unstable data
- **2. Decide whether a tool default is actually defensible for this dataset**:
  - Defaults are a starting point only when the dataset facts do not
    already argue against them.
- **3. Name the actual uncertainty**:
  - analysis mode
  - fragment / extension assumption
  - significance threshold
  - duplicate policy
  - paired-end concordance / mate-handling policy
  - mitochondrial or low-quality alignment filtering
  - background/local-bias correction
- **4. Compare a small plausible set**:
  - Change one uncertainty family at a time unless the task truly
    requires coupled changes.
  - If one candidate came from warning text, compare it against another
    plausible value grounded in task facts before accepting it.
- **5. Accept only a branch you can explain**:
  - A non-default choice must be justified by task facts, assay context,
    or a controlled comparison.

## Key Rules

- **Task and data context outranks tool suggestions**.
- **A tool warning gives diagnosis, not prescription**.
- **Check the dataset before privileging a default**.
- **"More stringent" is not automatically better science**.
- **If provenance is unclear, stop rather than substitute data from a
  different run branch**.

## Avoid These Mistakes

- Avoid directly using a parameter value just because a tool warning suggested it; first decide whether that value fits this dataset.
- Avoid downloading outputs from an old history just because you could not create a fresh run; stop or retry cleanly instead.
- Avoid responding to a sparse result by automatically making the threshold stricter; first decide which uncertainty actually needs testing.
- Avoid relaxing q-value, duplicate policy, shift, and extension all at once when a result looks weak; keep causal control.
- Avoid assuming that more output means a better result; check whether the result is actually more plausible.
- Avoid disabling local background or bias correction as an unexamined shortcut; if you turn it off, verify that the result did not become over-permissive.
- Avoid changing paired-end handling, mapping-quality filtering,
  mitochondrial filtering, duplicate policy, and peak threshold together
  without showing which change fixed the problem.
- Avoid replacing a task-provided whole-reference parameter with a subset-only
  value just because the input reads are enriched for one chromosome; use the
  task/reference scope unless there is a specific reason to change it.

run_trace/galaxy_tool_run_003/validation_response.json:14:  "help": "<p><strong>PepQuery2</strong></p>\n<p><a class=\"reference external\" href=\"http://pepquery.org/document.html\">PepQuery</a> is a universal targeted peptide search engine for identifying or validating known and novel peptides of interest in any local or publicly available mass spectrometry-based proteomics datasets.</p>\n<p><a class=\"reference external\" href=\"http://pepquery.org/document.html\">PepQuery</a> is a peptide-centric search engine for novel peptide identification and validation. Cancer genomics studies have identified a large number of genomic alterations that may lead to novel, cancer-specific protein sequences. Proteins resulted from these genomic alterations are attractive candidates for cancer biomarkers and therapeutic targets. The leading approach to proteomic validation of genomic alterations is to analyze tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) data using customized proteomics databases created from genomics data. Such analysis is time-consuming and requires thorough training and detailed knowledge in proteomics data analysis, leading to a gap between MS/MS data and the cancer genomics community. PepQuery does not require customized databases and allows quick and easy proteomic validation of genomic alterations.</p>\n<p>PepQuery2 leverages a new MS/MS indexing approach and cloud storage to enable ultrafast, targeted identification of both novel and known peptides. PepQuery2 allows users to search more than one billion MS/MS data indexed in the PepQueryDB from any computers with internet access. It also supports direct analysis of user provided MS/MS data, any public datasets in PRIDE, MassIVE, jPOSTrepo and iProX, or Universal Spectrum Identifiers (USIs) from ProteomeXchange.</p>\n<dl class=\"docutils\">\n<dt><strong>Inputs</strong></dt>\n<dd><ul class=\"first last\">\n<li><p class=\"first\">A sequence to match, one of the following:</p>\n<ul class=\"simple\">\n<li>A peptide string (or strings separated by commas)</li>\n<li>A history dataset with a list of peptides</li>\n<li>A protein string or a history dataset with a protein fasta</li>\n<li>A DNA string that is at least 60 base pairs in length</li>\n</ul>\n</li>\n<li><p class=\"first\">MS/MS data used for identification, one of the following:</p>\n<ul>\n<li><p class=\"first\">Mass Spectrometry history datasets in MGF, mzML, or mzXML format</p>\n</li>\n<li><p class=\"first\">An Indexed MS/MS dataset  (from previous PepQuery2 run or from <strong>PepQuery2 index</strong> tool.)</p>\n</li>\n<li><p class=\"first\">PepQueryDB dataset IDs</p>\n<!--  -->\n<p>Multiple datasets from PepQueryDB must be separated by comma.
